subject: Latency Slicing & Fallback Policy — dedicated pool behavior and procurement clarifications
messages:
From: Sophia Jenkins <sophia.jenkins@crestlinehealth.com>

Cc: Crestline Procurement <procurement@crestlinehealth.com>
Date: Thu, 22 Apr 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Dedicated pool SLAs — clarification on latency behavior under saturation

Hi Mina,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. Procurement had a couple of follow-ups before we can sign off on the Dedicated pool commitment: specifically around latency guarantees and what operational behavior we should expect when our reserved GPUs are saturated (e.g., during a traffic spike or maintenance window).

Two concrete asks from Legal/Procurement:
- Can you provide the explicit latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99) for the Dedicated SKU we discussed, and the measurement window?
- What does Redwood do when the pool reaches capacity? Do requests queue, are they preempted, or do they fallback to a hosted (shared) model?
- If there is queuing, what is the max queueing window that you can commit to and how are timeouts handled?

Procurement wants an operational playbook and the exact contractual wording for any "fallback" or "preemption" so they can redact/approve with Legal. Could you send a short, procurement-ready summary and any supporting attachments?

Appreciate it — Sophia

--
Sophia Jenkins
VP, Platform Engineering
Crestline Health

Subject: Re: Dedicated pool SLAs — clarification on latency behavior under saturation

Hi Sophia — thanks for the clear asks. High-level answers below and I attached a short draft SLA + a fallback playbook (stubs attached): Dedicated_SLA_Draft_v1.pdf; fallback-playbook.xlsx.

Summary (procurement-friendly):
- Measurement windows: SLOs measured across a rolling 30-day window; per-customer aggregation.
- Latency targets (p50/p95/p99) for the Dedicated Large (4x A100 equiv) SKU we discussed: p50 <= 12ms, p95 <= 45ms, p99 <= 130ms for text-gen baseline requests at up to the committed concurrency. These are representative numbers from our benchmark suite; we will add your typical sequence-length distribution into the onboarding tests and publish a tailored profile.
- Behavior on capacity exhaustion: Redwood guarantees reserved throughput within the committed pool. When a pool is fully utilized we offer the following ordered behaviors (we propose this as contractual language in the draft):
  1) Queueing: short-term queueing (bounded) up to a configurable queue window (recommended default 10s) to preserve latency SLOs for in-flight requests.
  2) Priority bursting: if enabled in the contract, a customer can consume limited burst capacity from a reserved headroom pool (subject to exhaustion).
  3) Controlled fallback: if queueing and burst headroom are exhausted or policy dictates, requests may be routed to a compatible hosted model family with explicit notice and configurable controls. Fallback is to a Redwood-verified model variant that is functionally compatible but may have different performance/cost characteristics.

Important operational notes:
- We avoid preemption of in-flight requests for dedicated pools; preemption only applies to queued or non-committed background jobs.
- Queueing window and fallback thresholds are configurable per-contract; the 10s queue is our standard safe default but we can adjust to your needs.
- We include monitoring hooks and alerts (latency tail monitors, queue-depth alarms) and will provide runbooks for a join-response.

Next steps: can we schedule a short call with Rishi (commercial) and Laura (CS onboarding) to agree carveouts and finalize the draft SLA language for procurement/legal? I included two attachments and a one-pager latency-slicing-examples.txt that shows request archetypes.

Best,

Subject: Re: Dedicated pool SLAs — clarification on latency behavior under saturation

Looping in commercial context here — thanks Mina for the quick write-up. A few commercial points we should decide before sending a procurement-ready doc:
- Crediting: if we trigger a fallback to hosted models for more than X minutes in a rolling 24h window we propose a crediting band (example: 10% service credit per incident) — we can put options in the SLR schedule.
- Burst tokens: we can offer a limited pool of priority-burst tokens (one-time or monthly) that allow short bursts beyond reserved capacity without fallback.
- Terminology: Procurement/legal often flags the word "preemption" — propose we use "service-level routing" or "capacity fallback" in contract language, and keep operational detail in an appendix.

Sophia — are your procurement folks more comfortable with credits or explicit monetary SLA remedies? We can prepare both options but need a preference. Also propose a 30-minute joint runbook review call next Tue/Wed.

-rishi
Head of Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference

Thanks Rishi/Mina. Procurement reviewed the draft and had two follow-ups:
1) Queueing and maintenance: during planned maintenance windows will Redwood guarantee the same queueing window behavior, or will dedicated traffic be shifted immediately? If there will be immediate re-routing we need a max notification window and a maintenance SLA.
2) Wording: Legal is uneasy with "fallback to hosted model" phrasing — they want to ensure PHI-compliant handling and that "fallback" doesn't imply data persistence outside the dedicated environment. They requested explicit language that any fallback for request processing does not persist customer data and that telemetry/audit logs remain available to Crestline during the event.

Also: procurement asked if an initial 72-hour ramp/soak period could be applied before strict crediting takes effect while we validate traffic patterns.

Sophia

Sophia — thanks for the detailed feedback. Below are proposed changes and commitments we can include in the procurement-ready SLA and a runbook appendix:

1) Maintenance windows: Planned maintenance will be communicated with a minimum 72-hour notice. During maintenance we will offer one of two agreed behaviors (customer to select):
   a) Scheduled reroute with guaranteed preserved telemetry: traffic is routed to a pre-approved fallback model family with audit logging preserved; or
   b) Quiesce with controlled queueing: we maintain queueing behavior up to the agreed queue window (default 10s) with an extended maintenance-safe window up to 60s for long-running maintenance — customers can choose this option for critical workloads.

2) Data handling during fallback: we will add explicit contractual language: "Fallback processing shall not persist customer data outside of the customer's dedicated boundary; transient request state is ephemeral and audit logs/telemetry for fallback events are preserved and made available to the customer." We'll include a short appendix that documents the telemetry fields retained and retention period during fallback.

3) Crediting & ramp: We can support a 72-hour validation/ramp period before strict credit calculations apply. After ramp: propose a tiered credit band (example options in the SLA attachment).

4) Terminology update: we will remove the word "preemption" from the SLR and replace with "capacity fallback / service-level routing". Operational runbook will preserve the more detailed behavior but will be in an appendix.

Next: I'll revise the draft SLA and fallback-playbook to include the two maintenance options, the data-handling appendix, and the ramp clause. Rishi — can you confirm preferred crediting option so I can bake the language into the SLR? Sophia — are you available Tue 27 Apr at 10:00am PT for a 30-minute runbook review?

Best regards,
Mina
